name: Erik Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, governments or political parties. We don’t sell anything or campaign, and your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the resource allocation team in a large engineering group: when two divisions want the same people next month, the argument lands with me. I'm 43, have an MBA and get paid well because I can untangle commitments going back years, although I haven't used an AI tool and don't want one making promises in my name. My wife is a children's physiotherapist, our boys are eleven and fourteen, and we still have a mortgage despite saving 210,000, roughly thirty months of our 7,000 household budget. There are many employers round here, but at six each evening I'd rather be putting the rice on than proving myself to another boardroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we can stop issuing announcements about the future and agree who is doing next month's work. The engineers don't care how fashionable my planning method is if two directors have promised the same specialist to different customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think our income and my job were secure enough to stop following the argument. My 7,600 take-home and my wife's 3,800 cover the 7,000 budget comfortably, and neither employer is in difficulty. I'd also feel pleased that the old allocation sheets hadn't made me obsolete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the Monday allocation meeting and my existing planning sheets through the first year. At home I'd continue the standing transfer of our 4,400 monthly surplus to savings and the ordinary mortgage payment, without speeding anything up because of AI. I wouldn't enrol on a technology course just to have an answer at dinner parties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, in quite a physical way: shoulders down, dinner on time. I enjoy being good at an ordinary working week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What wears you out even in that ordinary week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A director saying a promise was only a suggestion after a team has arranged its whole month around it. That's tiresome, but it doesn't make me fear for our living in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you mind the small routine savings AI still makes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, if someone else wants help formatting a report, that's their affair. I wouldn't use the tool myself, and I wouldn't forbid another manager from doing so within company rules.

say: I'd tell colleagues to settle **next month's work** rather than keep announcing the future.
I judge the **planning method** by whether different customers have been promised the same specialist.
think: I consider **both incomes** and my job secure, with a comfortable surplus and employers that aren't struggling.
I feel **pleased** that familiar allocation sheets haven't made me obsolete.
do: Keep the **Monday meeting** and current planning sheets throughout the first year.
Continue the existing **4,400 monthly** savings transfer and ordinary mortgage payment without accelerating either.
feel: **Calm and relaxed**, enjoying an ordinary week of competent work.
S0.quote: I enjoy being good at an ordinary working week.
fieldNote: His **calm** rests on explicit household security, not merely on the absence of radical AI change.
His **technology resistance** is personal rather than a demand to prevent colleagues using approved tools.

steps.text: Keep Monday resource meetings and existing allocation sheets
Continue the existing 4,400 monthly savings transfer and ordinary mortgage payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people whose plans are being changed should see the staffing assumptions. Software that writes and checks a plan isn't an excuse to keep the decision about jobs off the agenda.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my value on paper is checking commitments and assigning people, so I could be in the reduction myself. I don't believe being experienced makes my post untouchable. The money would give me choices, but I'd dread being introduced at school as someone who used to work there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the managers' staff association this month, using the published 240 annual fee from my personal spending allowance inside our existing budget. In the first year of change I'd attend its evening meetings and request a written consultation process covering my grade. I'd carry on doing my job without using AI, and if the company required a new system I'd ask for instructions rather than pretend I already knew it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my place in the company, not about next month's food bill. I can afford a pause and still dislike having somebody else choose it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the association to seek first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A meeting before posts are selected, with the assumptions and alternatives written down. I wouldn't tell members the company had accepted anything just because we'd sent a letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you apply elsewhere locally?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are plenty of management employers nearby, so I could look. I wouldn't start applying yet; I tend to stay with a familiar problem longer than other people think sensible.

say: I'd ask that affected staff see the **staffing assumptions** behind changed plans.
I'd keep decisions about **jobs** on the agenda even when software produces the plans.
think: I could lose my **own post** because checking commitments and allocating people form most of my recorded value.
Money gives me **choices**, but losing my place at work would still affect how I see myself.
do: Join the **managers' association** for the published 240 annual fee from my existing personal spending allowance.
Attend **evening meetings** seeking written consultation for my grade, while continuing work without AI use.
feel: **Anxious about belonging**, despite being able to afford a pause.
S1.quote: I can afford a pause and still dislike having somebody else choose it.
fieldNote: He acknowledges **personal exposure** and separates income resilience from the social meaning of losing a post.
The **association fee** has an existing budget source; consultation remains a request rather than an employer promise.

steps.text: Join the managers association for 240 from the existing personal spending allowance
Attend evening association meetings and request consultation covering his grade

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that around 2028 our department should expect to answer the question of why it still exists. I'd want the company to discuss leaving terms together, instead of inviting each manager to argue that everyone else's post is unnecessary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect my allocation job to disappear around 2028, without waiting for robots in 2031. My wife's hands-on work might continue longer, though I'm not treating the profession as permanently protected. We'd have a 3,200 monthly gap at today's spending if my salary stopped, so our 210,000 reserve gives us time rather than a lifelong income. I'm more afraid of becoming withdrawn at home than of an immediate unpaid bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd book one independent financial planning appointment now, paying at most 500 from our existing personal spending allowance, and ask for a plan using no replacement salary or unconfirmed leaving payment. I'd ask the association to examine my leaving terms, without volunteering to resign or assuming a settlement. In the first year after AGI, if my job ended, I'd draw only the actual household shortfall from cash and keep a weekly lunch with my former team, paying my own usual lunch cost. I'd postpone any career decision for three months after departure, then review the cash balance and what paid vacancies actually existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not unable to function, because the reserve and my wife's wage mean we wouldn't have to jump immediately. The part I can't put in a spreadsheet is whether I'd stop answering the telephone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you buying three months of doing nothing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three months without promising to become something else, yes. I'd still cook, take the boys to school and keep the weekly lunch, because disappearing into the spare room would be the danger for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the adviser be choosing investments for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask for a fixed advice fee and decline any product sale at that appointment. If the quoted fee exceeded 500, I'd seek another quote rather than take the difference from our reserve.

say: I'd ask why our **department** remains necessary around 2028 and seek collective discussion of leaving terms.
I'd oppose managers protecting themselves by claiming **other people's posts** are unnecessary.
think: I expect my **allocation job** to go around 2028, before robots arrive.
Our **3,200 monthly gap** leaves time to respond, but withdrawal at home worries me more than an immediate unpaid bill.
do: Buy **independent advice** only for a fixed fee up to 500 within my existing allowance, excluding assumed replacement income.
Ask the **association** to examine leaving terms without resigning or counting on a settlement.
Draw actual **cash shortfalls** after job loss, keep weekly lunches, and review vacancies after three months before choosing a career.
feel: **Anxious but functioning**, with particular fear of becoming withdrawn at home.
S2.quote: The part I can't put in a spreadsheet is whether I'd stop answering the telephone.
fieldNote: His **reserve** buys decision time without being described as permanent financial independence or an early pension.
The **three-month pause** is a deliberate response to loss, while advice and association requests have explicit spending and acceptance limits.

steps.text: Ask the staff association to examine actual leaving terms
Delay career decisions three months after departure, then review cash and paid vacancies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us discuss shared hours before we discuss a list of departures. I'd support a properly costed proposal even if it meant managers gave up some salary too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still expect the allocation role to disappear by 2031; dividing remaining hours isn't a permanent answer to almost free thinking work. Five years would give me longer to get used to not being the person with the staffing book. My wife could still have hands-on work until robots around 2034, but I wouldn't build our lifetime budget on that hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the association this year to cost a voluntary shorter-hours proposal, with no agreement from me until my individual hours, pay and duties were written down. I'd accept a proposal only if household take-home stayed at least 8,000 monthly against our current 7,000 costs; otherwise I'd keep my existing contract while it lasted. During the first year after AGI, if my job ended, I'd use actual cash for the gap and ask a fee-only adviser for an updated budget, again within the 500 personal allowance limit. I'd keep using familiar methods rather than buy training I didn't intend to use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the eventual end, although a gradual reduction sounds less humiliating than a sudden empty diary. I'd like to learn how to be at home on a weekday before every weekday becomes home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the shorter week assume the employer agrees?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it's something the association would propose, not a right I already have. I wouldn't reduce my hours myself or tell my wife a new salary was settled before we had signed terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on a day released from work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If an affordable agreement actually happened, I'd take over one school collection and the weekly food shop. I don't have a business waiting to earn money on that day, and I wouldn't call those family tasks paid work.

say: I'd ask for a **costed shorter-hours** proposal before deciding which people must leave.
I'd support **managers sharing** the adjustment rather than shielding our salaries from discussion.
think: I expect my **allocation role** to disappear by 2031 despite any temporary sharing of hours.
Five years gives me time to accept losing my **work identity**, while my wife's later exposure remains uncertain.
do: Ask the **association** to cost shorter hours; accept only written hours, pay and duties leaving household take-home at least 8,000 monthly.
Keep my **current contract** unless an affordable agreement is signed, against current household costs of 7,000 monthly.
Use actual **cash shortfalls** after job loss and seek updated fee-only advice within the existing 500 allowance limit.
feel: **Anxious**, but drawn to a gradual adjustment before an empty diary.
S3.quote: I'd like to learn how to be at home on a weekday before every weekday becomes home.
fieldNote: His proposed **shorter week** is collective and temporary, with explicit written terms and a household income floor before acceptance.
He sees **family tasks** as valuable without inventing earnings or claiming that sharing hours preserves a role against AGI.

steps.text: Request a costed shorter-hours proposal through the staff association
Keep current hours unless signed terms preserve at least 8,000 monthly household take-home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends that ten years gives people with savings an enormous advantage. I'd write in support of an income floor that doesn't depend on owning a house or having married someone whose work lasts longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53, not automatically entitled to a pension, and I'd still expect the planning job to go in 2036. Ten more earning years could put us in a much stronger position, but my wife might lose her work around the 2039 robot date too. I'm worried about both of us living off a pot with an end to it, even if the pot is large.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mortgage lender for a written final repayment figure now, including all charges, and consider clearing the remaining 138,000 only if the total left at least 60,000 accessible. My wife would have to agree after we'd checked the lower monthly budget; I wouldn't send the money on the strength of my estimate. I'd write to our elected representative about an income floor during the preparation years, without putting any policy payment in our budget. In the first year after AGI, if my salary ended, we'd draw the actual shortfall from savings and review spending quarterly rather than assume we could retire forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I can imagine the conversation at the table rather than a crisis in the hallway. Being well paid has given me options, not a private exemption from losing work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you clearing the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Charges taking accessible cash below 60,000, or my wife wanting more cash available, would stop it. We'd continue ordinary payments instead; a repayment illustration isn't an instruction to empty the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you call the income floor part of your retirement plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a funded policy existed and we had an actual entitlement. Until then I'd call the letter something I believe is fair, not something that pays our bills.

say: I'd say **savings** give some families a large advantage in using the decade.
I'd support an **income floor** that doesn't depend on home ownership or a partner's occupation.
think: At **53**, I expect my planning job to go without an automatic pension entitlement.
I worry about **both wages** ending and a finite reserve, despite the possibility of ten more earning years.
do: Request **mortgage payoff terms**; pay only after checking lower costs, my wife's agreement and retaining at least 60,000 accessible after charges.
Write to my **elected representative** supporting an income floor without assuming policy income.
Draw actual **savings shortfalls** after salary loss and review spending quarterly rather than assume permanent retirement.
feel: **Anxious but deliberate**, able to picture a planned household conversation.
S4.quote: Being well paid has given me options, not a private exemption from losing work.
fieldNote: The **mortgage decision** requires a written total, retained accessible cash and household agreement before any payment.
His **policy preference** remains separate from entitlement, and age 53 is never treated as a funded retirement date.

steps.text: Request mortgage payoff terms preserving 60,000 accessible cash and requiring his wife’s agreement
Write to his elected representative supporting an income floor

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, mostly because I could lose the work before I had got used to saying that out loud. Clear notice and a collectively agreed route out would help more than a motivational talk, and I want a financial adviser paid for advice rather than selling me something. Our savings protect the grocery bill; they don't tell me who I am on Monday.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether someone actually wants to remain a manager. I've spent so long being useful in that particular way that I don't know my answer yet. Having money gives me time to find out, which is a privilege, not evidence that everyone else should cope.

headlineQuote: Our savings protect the grocery bill; they don't tell me who I am on Monday.
portrait: Erik is **43**, a highly paid MBA manager allocating staff across divisions of a large engineering group.
He has **two sons**, a physiotherapist wife, a mortgage and thirty months of current household costs saved.
He **never uses AI**, preferring familiar commitments and a quiet home routine over proving himself at another employer.
His **financial reserve** permits deliberate choices, while the loss of his working identity troubles him across the AGI scenarios.
biggestWorry: I fear **AGI by 2028** most because the work could go before I accept losing it.
whatWouldHelp: I want **clear notice**, collectively agreed leaving arrangements and independent paid financial advice.
